nodes.name: Log-concave and log-convex sequences
nodes.statement: Let $\{z_n\}_{n\geq0}$ be a sequence of positive numbers. It is called {\it log-concave} (resp. {\it log-convex}) if $z_{n-1}z_{n+1}\le z_n^2$ (resp. $z_{n-1}z_{n+1}\ge z_n^2$) for all $n\ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: A positive sequence is log-concave (log-convex) if $z_{n-1}z_{n+1}\le z_n^2$ ($\ge$) for all $n\ge1$.

nodes.name: Ratio criterion for log-concavity
nodes.statement: Clearly, the sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is log-concave (resp. log-convex) if and only if the sequence $\{z_{n+1}/z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is decreasing (resp. increasing).
conclusions: the sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is log-concave (resp. log-convex) if and only if the sequence $\{z_{n+1}/z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is decreasing (resp. increasing)
nodes.statement_short: A sequence is log-concave (log-convex) iff its successive ratios decrease (increase).

nodes.name: Wang-Zhu criterion for monotonicity of $\sqrt[n]{z_n}$
nodes.statement: For example, for a positive log-convex sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$, if $z_0\le 1$, then the sequence $\{\sqrt[n]{z_n}\}_{n\ge 1}$ is increasing.

nodes.name: Monotonicity criterion for $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be a positive number. If $f(x)$ is a positive increasing log-convex function for $x\geq N$ and $f(N)\leq 1$, then $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is strictly increasing on $(N,\infty)$.
assumptions: $f(x)$ is a positive increasing log-convex function for $x\geq N$
nodes.statement_short: If $f$ is positive, increasing and log-convex on $[N,\infty)$ with $f(N)\le1$, then $f(x)^{1/x}$ strictly increases.
nodes.label: thm+inc

nodes.name: Applications of the monotonicity criterion
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm+inc} can be applied to the monotonicity of $\{\sqrt[n]{z_n}\}_{n\ge 1}$ for some combinatorial sequences $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$. Some further examples and applications related to Theorem~\ref{thm+inc} can be found in \cite{CGW}.

nodes.name: Bernoulli numbers and the function theta
nodes.statement: Recall that the classical Bernoulli numbers are defined by $$B_0=1,\quad \sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n+1}{k}B_k=0,\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.$$ It is well known that $B_{2n+1}=0, (-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}>0$ for $n\ge 1$ and $$(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}=\frac{2(2n)!\zeta(2n)}{(2\pi)^{2n}},$$ see \cite[(6.89)]{GKP94} for instance. In order to show that $\{\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}\}$ is increasing, Chen et al \cite{CGW} introduced the function $\theta(x)=\sqrt[x]{2 \zeta(x)\Gamma(x+1)},$ where $$\zeta(x)=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{1}{n^x}$$ is the Riemann zeta function and $\Gamma(x)$ is the Euler Gamma function. Thus $$\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}={\theta^2(2n)}/{4\pi^{2}}.$$ They proved that $\theta(x)$ is increasing on $(6,\infty)$. In addition, in order to get the log-concavity of $\{\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}\}_{n\ge 1}$, they further conjectured. \begin{conj}\emph{\cite{CGW}} The function $\theta(x)=\sqrt[x]{2 \zeta(x)\Gamma(x+1)}$ is log-concave on $(6,\infty)$. \end{conj}
nodes.statement_short: Bernoulli numbers via $\zeta$; Chen et al.'s function $\theta(x)=\sqrt[x]{2\zeta(x)\Gamma(x+1)}$ and their log-concavity conjecture.

nodes.name: Operator $R$
nodes.statement: Moreover, they introduced a stronger concept as follows: define an operator $R$ on a sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ by $$R\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}=\{x_n\}_{n\geq 0},$$ where $x_n = z_{n+1}/{z_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: The ratio operator $R$ maps $\{z_n\}$ to $\{z_{n+1}/z_n\}$.

nodes.name: Infinitely log-monotonic sequence
nodes.statement: The sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is called {\it infinitely log-monotonic} if the sequence $R^r\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is log-concave for all positive odd $r$ and is log-convex for all nonnegative even $r$.
differentia: the sequence $R^r\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is log-concave for all positive odd $r$
is log-convex for all nonnegative even $r$
nodes.statement_short: $\{z_n\}$ is infinitely log-monotonic if $R^r\{z_n\}$ is log-concave for odd $r>0$ and log-convex for even $r\ge0$.

nodes.name: Completely monotonic function
nodes.statement: Recall that a function $f(x)$ is said to be {\it completely monotonic} on an interval $I$ if $f(x)$ has derivatives of all orders on $I$ which alternate successively in sign, that is, $$(-1)^nf^{(n)}(x)\geq0$$ for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 0$.
differentia: $f(x)$ has derivatives of all orders on $I$ which alternate successively in sign
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is completely monotonic on $I$ if $(-1)^n f^{(n)}\ge0$ on $I$ for all $n\ge0$.

nodes.name: Strictly completely monotonic function
nodes.statement: If inequality is strict for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 0$, then $f(x)$ is said to be strictly completely monotonic.

nodes.name: Logarithmically completely monotonic function
nodes.statement: A positive function $f(x)$ is said to be {\it logarithmically completely monotonic} on an interval $I$ if $\log f(x)$ satisfies $$(-1)^n[\log f(x)]^{n}\geq0$$ for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 1$.
differentia: $$(-1)^n[\log f(x)]^{n}\geq0$$ for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 1$
nodes.statement_short: A positive $f$ is logarithmically completely monotonic if $(-1)^n(\log f)^{(n)}\ge0$ for all $n\ge1$.

nodes.name: Logarithmically completely monotonic implies completely monotonic
nodes.statement: A logarithmically completely monotonic function is completely monotonic, but not vice versa, see Berg~\cite{Ber04}.
conclusions: A logarithmically completely monotonic function is completely monotonic, but not vice versa

nodes.name: Proof of the monotonicity criterion
nodes.statement: \quad Let $y=\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$. Then one can get \begin{equation*} y'=\frac{y}{x}\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}-\frac{\log{f(x)}}{x}\right). \end{equation*} In order to show that $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is strictly increasing, it suffices to prove \begin{equation} \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}-\frac{\log{f(x)}}{x}>0 \end{equation} for $x\geq N$. Since $f(N)\leq 1$ and $f(x)$ is increasing, one can derive that \begin{equation} \frac{\log{f(x)}}{x}\leq\frac{\log{f(x)}-\log{f(N)}}{x}<\frac{\log{f(x)}-\log{f(N)}}{x-N} \end{equation} for $x\geq N$. By the mean value theorem, one can obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\log{f(x)}-\log{f(N)}}{x-N}=\frac{f'(\xi)}{f(\xi)}, \end{equation} where $N\leq\xi\leq x$. On the other hand, it follows from log-convexity of the function $f(x)$ that \begin{equation} \left(\log{f(x)}\right)''=\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right)'=\frac{f''(x)f(x)-f'(x)^2}{f^2(x)}\geq0, \end{equation} which implies that $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ is increasing. Thus, it follows that \begin{equation} \frac{f'(\xi)}{f(\xi)}\leq\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \end{equation} for $x\geq\xi.$ Combining (\ref{e2}), (\ref{e3}) and (\ref{e4}), one can obtain (\ref{e1}). So $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is increasing.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: From (\ref{e}), one can deduce $$\frac{n!}{e}-\frac{1}{2}\leq d_n\leq \frac{n!}{e}+\frac{1}{2},$$ which implies $$\Gamma(n+1)-\frac{3}{2}\leq e d_n\leq \Gamma(n+1)+\frac{3}{2}.$$ Thus \begin{eqnarray*} &&e^2(d_{n+1}d_{n-1}-d_n^2)\\ &\geq&[\Gamma(n+2)-1.5][\Gamma(n)-1.5]-[\Gamma(n+1)+1.5]^2\\ &>0& \end{eqnarray*} for $n\ge4$, which implies that $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 4}$ is log-convex. Note that \begin{eqnarray*} &&e^4(d_{n+1}^3d_{n-1}-d_{n}^3d_{n+2})\\ &\geq&[\Gamma(n+2)-1.5]^3[\Gamma(n)-1.5]-[\Gamma(n+1)+1.5]^3[\Gamma(n+3)+1.5]\\ &>0& \end{eqnarray*} for $n\ge8$, which implies that $R\{d_n\}_{n\geq 8}$ is log-concave. Because $\{\Gamma(n)\}_{n\geq1}$ is strictly infinitely log-monotonic, similarly, it can be proceeded to the higher order log-monotonicity. Thus, for any positive integer $k $, by the sign-preserving property of limits, one can obtain that there exists a positive $N$ such that the sequence $R^r\{d_n\}_{n\geq N}$ is log-concave for positive odd $r$ and is log-convex for positive even $r$. Thus, the sequence of the derangements numbers $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is asymptotically infinitely log-monotonic.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.6
nodes.statement: Since $$\log\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)=-\frac{\log\left(a\zeta(x+b)\Gamma(x+c)\right)}{x}=-\frac{\log a+\log\zeta(x+b)+\log\Gamma(x+c)}{x},$$ in order to show that $\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,\infty)$, it suffices to prove $$(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)\geq0$$ for all $n\geq1$. Note that a known formula as follows: \begin{eqnarray} \left(\frac{g(x)}{x}\right)^{(n)}=\frac{(-1)^ng(0)n!}{x^{n+1}}+x^{-n-1}\int_0^x t^n g^{(n+1)}(x)dt, \end{eqnarray} which can be easily proved by induction. nodes.name: Derivative formula
nodes.statement: Define the function $h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log \Gamma(x+a_i)-\log\Gamma(x+b_i)$. Then $$\log\sqrt[x]{\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}=\frac{\log\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}{x} =\frac{\log\rho+h(x)}{x}.$$ So it is not hard to get \begin{eqnarray} &&(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}=\frac{k!(\log\rho+h(0))}{x^{k+1}}+x^{-k-1}\int_0^x t^k (-1)^kh^{(k+1)}(x)dt. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $h$ and derive formula (4.5).

nodes.name: Boundary term
nodes.statement: If $\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(a_i)}{\Gamma(b_i)}\geq1$, then it is clear that $$\log\rho+h(0)\geq0.$$
nodes.statement_short: The boundary term is nonnegative.

nodes.name: Alzer's sign result
nodes.statement: In addition, Alzer \cite{Al97} proved that $(-1)^kh^{(k+1)}(x)\geq0$ for $k\geq0$ and $x\geq0$.
nodes.statement_short: Alzer's result gives the sign of the integrand.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus, $$(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}\geq0,$$ that is, $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude logarithmic complete monotonicity.

nodes.name: Special cases of Theorem 4.8
nodes.statement: If $\rho=2\sqrt{\pi}$, $a_1=1$ and $b_1=\frac{1}{2}$, then $\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(1)}{\Gamma(1/2)}=2>1$. So the function $\sqrt[x]{\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(x+1)}{\Gamma(x+1/2)}}$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$, see \cite{LT11}. In addition, if $n=1$ in Theorem~\ref{thm+comp}, then it was proved by Qi and Li \cite{QL13}. Thus, the result in Theorem~\ref{thm+comp} is a generalization.
nodes.statement_short: Lee-Tepedelenlioglu's coding-gain function and Qi-Li's result are special cases ($n=1$) of Theorem 4.8.
